1:
The psalm opens with a confession so familiar that the witnesses pause over almost every word of it, asking first who the shepherd is and when the song was sung. The reformed John Gill will not let the shepherd be Jehovah the Father, as the Targum makes him, but Jehovah the Son, to whom the office is most frequently ascribed: called and appointed to it by his Father, and abundantly qualified for it, being omniscient, and so knowing all his sheep and their maladies, and omnipotent, having all power in heaven and earth to protect and save, so that he is the great, the chief, and the good Shepherd. David calls him my shepherd, Gill notes, Christ having a right to him by his Father's gift. The latin-fathers voice hears the same Christ in the words: Augustine has the Church herself speak to him, ‘the Lord feedeth me, and I shall lack nothing,’ the Lord Jesus Christ being the Shepherd under whom she wants for nothing.

The reformed John Calvin draws the pastoral image toward its condition: God is a shepherd only to those who, touched with a sense of their own weakness and poverty, feel their need of his protection; and it is the more remarkable that David, excelling in power and riches, nevertheless frankly confessed himself a poor sheep, that he might have God for his shepherd. The puritan-evangelical witnesses press the note of experience and confidence. Matthew Henry remembers that David had himself been a shepherd, taken from following the ewes great with young (Ps. 78:70-71), and so knew by proof the tender care a good shepherd bears his flock, to which our Saviour seems to refer in John 10:11; and though David had once sent begging to Nabal and gone begging to Ahimelech, yet, owning God his shepherd, he can boldly say, ‘I shall not want.’ Charles Spurgeon dwells on the condescension that the Infinite Lord should take the shepherd's office, and on the sweetest word of the sentence, the monosyllable ‘my’: there is no ‘if’ nor ‘but’ nor even ‘I hope so,’ and the words stand in the present tense; for a man has no right to reckon himself the Lord's sheep, Spurgeon adds, whom grace has not renewed, the unconverted being in Scripture not sheep but wolves or goats.

The grammatical-historical witnesses set the psalm in its place. Charles Ellicott traces the shepherd-image applied to God, appearing first of his relation to the individual (Gen. 48:15; Gen. 49:24), then, more frequently, of his people (Isa. 40:11; Ezek. 34). Keil and Delitzsch admire the arrangement by which a psalm of a great feast prepared for mankind (Ps. 22) is followed by one praising Jahve as the Shepherd and Host of his own, and, holding David the author, refer it to the time of the rebellion under Absalom, when David yearned after the house of God. Against this the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke demurs: the psalm reads to him as a thanksgiving of redeemed captives, giving thanks for liberty and for access to the temple, and so ‘cannot with propriety be attributed to David,’ but was penned after the captivity. So the witnesses divide over the occasion even as they agree over the Shepherd, and over the boast the shepherd warrants, that his sheep shall not want.
2:
The shepherd's first office is to feed the flock and to settle it, and the witnesses take the two halves of the verse—the green pastures and the still waters—as the picture of a soul at rest. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the pastures as the ordinances of God, never barren, never eaten bare, always a green pasture for faith to feed in; the greatest abundance, he says, is but a dry pasture to a wicked man, who relishes only what pleases the senses, while to a godly man the least is green, for he tastes the goodness of God in all his enjoyments (Prov. 15:16-17). God makes his saints to lie down, giving them quiet and contentment whatever their lot; and the still waters are the consolations of God, the joys of the Holy Ghost, to which he leads them—not the standing waters that corrupt and gather filth, nor the troubled sea, nor the rapid rolling floods, but the silent purling waters that agree best with spirits flowing quietly toward God.

The reformed John Gill gives the pastures of tender grass a fuller, Christward sense: the covenant of grace and its promises, the fulness of grace in Christ, his flesh and blood and righteousness on which faith feeds, and the doctrines and ordinances of the Gospel, in which there is milk for babes and meat for strong men. To lie down in them, Gill adds, denotes satiety and fulness, and rest and safety too, these being sure dwellings and quiet resting-places even in the noon of temptation and persecution.

The wesleyan-arminian voices attend to the Hebrew and the landscape. Adam Clarke would not render the phrase ‘green pastures’ at all, but ‘cottages of turf or sods’ (binoth deshe), the folds where shepherds in open country could pen the flock safely and where grass was to be had; and by the ‘still waters’ he understands deep waters that the strongest heat could not exhale, no shallow rippling current, perhaps the softly-flowing waters of Shiloah set against the strong Euphrates (Isa. 8:6)—a figure, on his reading, of captives brought home from a turbulent land to their own quiet streams. John Wesley keeps it plainer: to lie down is to repose at noon, as the manner was in those hot countries, and ‘green’ means where there is both delight and plenty of provision. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott corrects the tense the English obscures: the verbs are not futures but presents, describing the poet's customary condition, the freshness of the meadow and the coolness of the stream making, as one writer he quotes has it, the most complete picture of happiness that ever was or can be drawn. The witnesses agree, then, on the rest while dividing over the scene—whether it be a literal fold and a deep, still pool, or the ordinances and consolations of God under the figure of grass and water.
3:
The care that feeds and leads now turns to healing and direction, and the witnesses weigh what it is in a man that the shepherd ‘restoreth.’ The reformed John Gill offers two senses without choosing sharply between them: the soul is restored when, backslidden, it is brought back and its wanderings healed; or, when fainting and swooning and ready to die away, it is fetched back and revived with the discoveries of God's love, the promises of his word, and the consolations of his Spirit. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry leans on the first: no creature will lose itself sooner than a sheep, nor is any so unapt to find its way back, and the best saints are sensible of their proneness to go astray like lost sheep (Ps. 119:176); when David's heart smote him, and again when Nathan was sent to tell him ‘Thou art the man,’ God restored his soul, for though he may suffer his people to fall into sin he will not suffer them to lie still in it. Yet Henry keeps Gill's second sense too, that God recovers the sick and revives the faint, being the Lord that heals us (Exod. 15:26).

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the restoring as conversion—bringing back the life from destruction and turning the soul from sin—and then strikes off on his own over the ‘paths of righteousness,’ which he renders the ‘circuits’ or ‘orbits of righteousness’ (bemageley tsedek). Man, on his figure, is like a secondary planet moving round its primary, or a planet round the sun, drawing all its light and heat from the Sun of righteousness; kept in his proper orbit he is enlightened and warmed and made fruitful, and can enlighten others in turn. John Wesley keeps the plainer road, glossing ‘restoreth’ as ‘he bringeth it back from its errors and wandering,’ and ‘for his name's sake’ as done not for any worth in us but for the glory of God's justice, faithfulness, and goodness. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott confirms the sense of the verb—it is to refresh, to recreate, to quicken—and takes ‘for his name's sake’ to mean that God's providential dealings answer to his own character for great graciousness. The witnesses do not finally divide; whether the restoring reclaim a wanderer or revive a fainting man, all agree that the leading which follows is into the paths of righteousness, the way of duty, which Henry calls the truly pleasant way, and that God both leads us into those paths and keeps us in them for his name's sake and not for our merit.
4:
‘Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil’—the most quoted line of the psalm draws the witnesses into three quarrels at once, over the words, the valley, and the rod. The reformed John Gill first clears away what the valley is not: not a state of spiritual darkness and ignorance, nor the hiding of God's face, since the psalmist here expressly says the Lord is with him; rather, since the grave is called the land of the shadow of death and the terrors of dying are called its shadow, the case supposed is that the soul should draw nigh to the grave and yet be fearless, singing ‘O death, where is thy sting?’—though best of all, Gill thinks, the words fit the most severe and terrible affliction or dark dispensation of Providence a man can pass under. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears the courage of a dying saint and finds four words that lessen the terror: it is but the shadow of death, and the shadow of a serpent cannot sting; it is a valley, and valleys are fruitful, death being fruitful of comforts to God's people; it is but a walk; and it is a walk through it, to the mountain of spices on the other side. Death is a king of terrors, he grants, but not to the sheep of Christ.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott raises the sharpest textual point. The famous phrase, to which Bunyan gave such reality, was probably on Hebrew lips no more than a forcible synonym for a dark, gloomy place, and the likelihood, he argues, is that instead of tsal-maveth, ‘shadow of death,’ we should read tsalmuth, ‘deep gloom’ or ‘darkness,’ the general sense being all that is required in any of the fifteen places the word occurs—of the grave (Job 10:21-22), the darkness of a dungeon (Ps. 107:10), or the pathless desert (Jer. 2:6); the valley itself he takes for a deep ravine, of the wild and gloomy sort in which Palestine abounds. Gill, Henry, and the rest keep the received ‘shadow of death.’ A second dispute follows over the rod. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke, holding the shepherd figure to the end—the flock passing through a dismal valley in the dead of night, among pitfalls and precipices and devouring beasts, safe only because the Shepherd knows every pass—insists that the rod (shebet, a staff of office) and the staff (a prop or support) are for guidance and defence and mean no correction at all: ‘they abuse the text,’ he says, ‘who paraphrase rod correction.’ John Wesley agrees that the two words denote one thing, God's pastoral care; Keil and Delitzsch call them Jahve's own rod and staff (Mic. 7:14), the one shepherd's rod under a double name, which preserve the feeling of security and a cheerful spirit. Against them the latin-fathers Augustine reads the rod as discipline—‘thy discipline, like a rod for a flock and a staff for growing children’—a chastening that has not been grievous but has comforted him. The witnesses agree only on the refrain that carries all their readings, ‘thou art with me’: it is the presence of the shepherd, not the smoothness of the valley, that takes the fear away.
5:
With the fifth verse the scene changes, and the witnesses dispute whether it changes altogether. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott calls the sudden transition from the figure of the flock to that of a banquet characteristic of Hebrew poetry: to ‘prepare’ is to spread or furnish a table (Prov. 9:2), the hospitable host being a familiar figure for God (Job 36:16; Isa. 25:6); the banquet he imagines spread on some secure mountain height, in sight of the baffled foe who look on in harmless spite. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke says outright that ‘here the second allegory begins’—a magnificent feast set out by a host who has both the bounty to provide and the power to protect, so that the guest, though surrounded by enemies, sits down in perfect security. The oil, Clarke notes, is the perfumed ointment poured on the heads of distinguished guests, as the woman poured her spikenard on the Lord's head, doing by custom what a neglectful host had failed to do (Luke 7:46); and the cup is filled to running over with the best wine.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, however, will not quite let the sheep go. Some think, he says, that David still looks on himself as a sheep, but such a one as the poor man's ewe-lamb that ate of his own meat and drank of his own cup and lay in his bosom (2 Sam. 12:3)—so tenderly, and not only so nobly, are the children of God looked after. Henry marks that the table is not spread with whatever came next to hand but prepared, and prepared before him; that the guest is not stinted but has his cup running over, enough for himself and his friends too; and that the oil is for ornament and delight, over and above necessity. The reformed John Gill spreads the one table over four rooms—the providential sufficiency God grants in the wilderness of this world, the goodness and fatness of his house in a way of grace, the table of the Lord under the Gospel, and the feast of heaven, of which the saints have here a foretaste. John Wesley, another wesleyan-arminian voice, keeps it short: the table is plenty of provision, the oil the aromatic ointment of great feasts whose comfort delights the soul, and the overflowing cup a plentiful portion handed by the master of the feast. Ellicott adds a last philological touch, that ‘my cup runneth over’ is literally ‘my cup is abundant drink,’ the cup standing, as often, for one's portion (Ps. 16:5). The witnesses divide, then, only over the frame: whether the shepherd has become a host and the flock guests at a feast, as Clarke and Ellicott have it, or whether, with Henry, the sheep is still a sheep, feasted at its owner's own table.
6:
The psalm gathers to its close on a note of certainty, and the witnesses find in its two clauses both a rich promise and a real question of translation. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears David's hope rise as his faith is exercised: he had said at the outset, ‘I shall not want,’ but now says more, that goodness and mercy—all the streams of it, pardoning, protecting, sustaining, supplying—shall follow him, and follow as the water out of the rock followed the camp of Israel through the wilderness, all his life long, new every morning like the manna (Lam. 3:22-23). And the last clause Henry reads as David's covenant, to dwell in God's house as long as he lives and praise him while he has any being, with a prospect beyond of removing to a better world, the Father's house above: ‘all this, and heaven too,’ he says; ‘then we serve a good Master.’ The reformed John Gill takes goodness and mercy for the free grace of God in Christ and its effects, temporal and spiritual alike, which follow his people undeserving of them, even when they have backslidden and in their times of distress.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch sharpen the image of pursuit: the foes who now pursue David shall be driven from the field, for goodness and favour alone shall pursue him, sent forth as good spirits by Jahve to overtake his enemies and guard him all his days. But over the closing line the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke presses a different reading. The verb, he says, is not ‘I will dwell’ but veshabti, ‘I shall return and abide in the house of the Lord’ for length of days—the very language, he thinks, of a priest brought back from captivity to serve God in the temple the rest of his life, and at last to dwell with him in glory. Ellicott, the other grammatical-historical voice, agrees that as the text stands it must be rendered ‘I will return and abide,’ and that the house of the Lord can hardly be anything but the Temple, though some take it figuratively of membership in the divine family; while Gill, Henry, and the reformed John Calvin—who ends the psalm ‘I shall dwell in the house of Jehovah for a length of days,’ making it David's resolve to give himself to God's pure worship—keep the familiar ‘dwell.’ So the psalm that began by owning one shepherd ends in a mild dispute over a single verb, whether the singer will dwell where he already is or return to the house he has been driven from; but the witnesses do not divide over the substance, that goodness and mercy will attend the man to the end, and the house of the Lord receive him for ever.
